analysis.one_liner: Bars states from banning IVF as a condition of receiving federal Medicaid money.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2024, referred to committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have told states that if they want federal Medicaid funding, they cannot prohibit in vitro fertilization (IVF), the fertility treatment in which eggs are fertilized outside the body. It would not have forced any doctor or organization to provide IVF, and it would not have required states to pay for IVF through Medicaid — it only would have blocked outright bans. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who need IVF to have children, roughly one in fifty births in the US today, would keep access to the treatment even in states inclined to restrict it. Fertility clinics and their patients would be protected from state bans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People trying to conceive via IVF

how_it_helps.text: States would lose federal Medicaid funding if they or any local government prohibited IVF services [S2].
The bill includes an explicit protection that no individual or organization can be forced to provide IVF, addressing conscience objections [S2].
States could still set health and safety standards for IVF; the bill blocks bans, not regulation [S2].
The bill's findings note that nearly 2 percent of all US live births result from IVF, meaning a ban would affect tens of thousands of births annually [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State governments that wanted to restrict IVF would face the loss of federal Medicaid money, the main funding stream for health coverage for low-income Americans. Taxpayers collectively bear no new cost, since the bill mandates nothing beyond permitting the practice.

drawbacks.text: The bill only blocks bans; it does not require Medicaid or any insurer to pay for IVF, which often costs patients tens of thousands of dollars out of pocket per attempt, so many people would remain unable to afford it [S2].

It attaches a condition to federal Medicaid payments, the money states use to cover low-income residents, which states that oppose the requirement could view as federal overreach into their authority over medical practice.
By not compelling anyone to provide IVF, the bill leaves room for providers or institutions to decline the service, which could limit practical access in some areas even where bans are blocked [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — guaranteeing that IVF stays legal everywhere — is real but narrow, because the bill does nothing about cost, and IVF is expensive enough that legality alone doesn't make it accessible to most people who need it. There is no meaningful cost to ordinary people; the burden falls only on states that would otherwise restrict the practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Scott Perry introduced the IVF Protection Act on June 27, 2024, with Representative Nancy Mace as a cosponsor [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete; the status quo held. States retained full authority to ban IVF, and policymakers inclined to restrict the procedure kept that option open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; states kept authority to ban IVF

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the IVF Protection Act in the House.

for.name: Rep. Nancy Mace
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; one of only two cosponsors total.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by Republicans, but only 2 of 224 House Republicans signed on and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of the issue was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed that IVF remains legal nationwide, protecting the industry's core market from state bans. Patients and clinics stood to win together, since the treatment is only available where it is legal. [S2] [S4]
